new_statements.quote: In Oc., as F. M. has remarked, the great mass of the stem-words are two-syllable, and the accent is on the first syllable. Of course I speak of the general rule in each case. [p.28] ... in Ef. minu with suffix i becomes minungi, in Sam. inu with suffix anga becomes inumanga, with suffix ia, inumia; as in its disappearance we see the influence of the accent, so in the reappearance of the final letter we also see the influence of the accent, for the suffixed particle draws the accent towards the end of the word. [p.29]
new_statements.citation: Macdonald, D. 1889. Oceania: linguistic and anthropological. Melbourne: M.L. Hutchinson; London: Sampson Low, Marston, Searle and Rivington.
new_statements.locator: Ch. II, pp. 28-29 ('influence of the accent'); cf. the same claim in Macdonald 1907, The Oceanic Languages, p. 51
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. File (Macdonald 1889, Oceania: linguistic and anthropological; archive.org djvu text; running heads '28 OCEANIA.' / '..ALPHABETIC CHARACTERS, ETC. 29' / '30 OCEANIA.'), lines 1824-1912. Both halves of the quoted passage are at the stated locator (pp. 28-29). Differences are scanned-level only: text reads 'In Oc, as F. M. has remarked' (no period after Oc), 'minungiy', 'inumangay', 'inuniia' for the first reader's cleaned 'In Oc.,', 'minungi', 'inumanga', 'inumia'; the first reader's ellipsis skips the Malay/Malagasy elision discussion. The 1907 cross-reference is also verbatim ( line ~2988, 'Remark on Ch. III.. bisyllabic words with the accent on the first s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Macdonald (creator of Efatese, 33 years at Havannah Harbour) states only a pan-'Oceanic' generalisation, credited to Friedrich Müller: stem-words are mostly disyllabic with the accent on the first syllable, and a suffix draws the accent toward the end of the word (illustrated with Efate minu -> minungi), a prefix away from it. Read literally for Efate words this amounts to a penultimate pattern (initial in disyllables, shifting right under suffixation), but 'penultimate' is my inference; he never states an accent rule for Efatese itself, and his Efatese grammar (1889), Efate dictionary (1894) and 1907 phonology chapter are silent on accent.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Of course I speak of the general rule in each case' (p.28); prefixes said to draw the accent away from the end of the word (p.30). No lexical exceptions given.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('stem-words' and suffixed words); statement is comparative/etymological, about 'Oceanic' generally with Efate and Samoan examples, not a synchronic description of Efatese. Efatese itself is a written compromise standard, so its 'stress' is that of the Efate vernaculars (nort2836/sout2856/lele1267).
new_statements.identity_note: efat1235 is not a spoken vernacular: it is the hybrid written Bible-translation language ("compromise literary dialect") assembled by the missionaries D. Macdonald (Havannah Harbour) and J.W. Mackenzie (Erakor) in the 1880s, mixing South Efate (sout2856), Nakanamanga/Nguna (nort2836) and Lelepa (lele1267) features (Thieberger & Ballard 2008). Macdonald's own 1889 sketch grammar states it gives 'the grammar of the Efatese as spoken in Havannah Harbour' (Lynch & Crowley 2001: 'actually Nakanamanga', nort2836). Any pronunciation/accent facts therefore belong to the underlying Efate vernaculars, which have their own glottocodes and modern descriptions (Schütz 1969 Nguna; Thieberger 2006 South Efate; Lacrampe 2014 Lelepa). Macdonald's only accent remarks are pan-'Oceanic' generalisations (crediting Friedrich Müller) illustrated with Efate and Samoan forms, embedded in his Semitic-origin theory.

sources.note: Pan-Oceanic: 'In Oc., as F. M. [Friedrich Müller] has remarked, the great mass of the stem-words are two-syllable, and the accent is on the first syllable' (p.28); suffixes draw the accent toward the end of the word, illustrated with Ef. minu -> minungi (p.29); prefixes draw it away from the end (p.30).
